title: 🎙️ Science, Wonder & the Natural World
description: Today we look at scientific discovery and the natural world — from ecology and wildlife research to astronomy and deep-sea biology. We're grounding these stories in the landscapes and living systems of the Cariboo: what salmon runs, boreal forest research, or species-at-risk studies tell us about the wild places we live beside. We're after stories that inspire curiosity and wonder about how the world works. - Daily themed article selection for podcast generation

_podcast.theme_description: Today we look at scientific discovery and the natural world — from ecology and wildlife research to astronomy and deep-sea biology. We're grounding these stories in the landscapes and living systems of the Cariboo: what salmon runs, boreal forest research, or species-at-risk studies tell us about the wild places we live beside. We're after stories that inspire curiosity and wonder about how the world works.
_podcast.theme_scoring_prompt: Rate how well this article fits the theme 'Science, Wonder & the Natural World' — scientific discovery, ecology, natural phenomena, and the curiosity-driven study of living systems. Strong fits include: wildlife biology and species research, ecology studies and biodiversity findings, watershed and salmon research relevant to BC, astronomy and space science, new species discoveries, citizen science projects, natural history stories, wildfire science and forest ecology, climate science findings (not just policy), geology, evolution, and deep-time Earth stories, and any scientific research grounded in BC or Cariboo landscapes and ecosystems. Prefer articles that convey genuine curiosity and discovery — the 'how' and 'why' of the natural world. Score 70–90 for: prehistoric life and palaeontology (ancient oceans, Cretaceous ecology, deep-time species), new species discoveries in ocean or remote environments, deep-sea biology, evolutionary biology findings, natural history stories with a strong sense of wonder, and field research grounded in BC ecosystems. Penalise (score 0–30): consumer health and pharmaceutical research without ecology or natural-world context; pure policy and advocacy news; technology business stories without a science or ecology angle; human interest and viral news without scientific substance; geopolitical and crime news. Score 0-100 where 100 is a perfect thematic match and 0 is completely unrelated.

Tanner Loring, 16, of Riske Creek is one of more than 700 young cowboys and cowgirls who will be heading to the entertainment capital of the world in December after qualifying for novice bull riding. In Williams Lake at the Bewitching Market on Saturday, Oct. 10, Linda could be found with Tanner’s great-aunt Ivy Bowe selling fresh frybread and fry dawgs. Sales that evening went towards paying for Linda and her husband, Loring’s grandfather, flight to Vegas to watch their grandson. “When I heard he was going to Vegas, I just hit every market I could to sell bread, and I’m doing quite well,” Linda said, adding that when her grandson is on television, she’s glued to the screen. In addition to the Bewitching Market, Linda also baked bread and buns to sell at various markets throughout the area over the summer. Bella Coola was where she was most successful with her sales, supporting their travel to Las Vegas. She has raised over $2,000. “We’re quite excited,” Linda said, adding she was able to watch Tanner compete in the B.C. Rodeo Association’s (BCRA) POLARIS Championship Finals Rodeo held at the 77th North Thompson Fall Fair & Rodeo in Barriere. items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

Use of death penalty against people for crimes committed when they were children a ‘new low’, say rights groups

A young man faces imminent execution in Saudi Arabia for attending protests and funerals when he was aged 15 to 17, say human rights groups, in the latest example of the kingdom’s surging use of the death penalty for non-violent crimes.

Youssef al-Manasif was arrested in 2017 and accused of crimes including joining demonstrations for religious freedom by the Shia minority and attending funerals that the Saudi authorities deem to be protests. He was convicted and sentenced to death by the specialised criminal court, a secretive tribunal set up for terrorism-related cases.

Prime Minister Mark Carney urged Albertans at a Calgary rally Thursday to vote to keep the province in Canada and reject nine other referendum proposals in the Oct. 19 vote [timescolonist.com#1][cbc.ca#1]. The ballot does not decide independence directly: it asks whether Alberta should remain in Canada or begin the legal process for a future binding separation referendum [oneindia.com#1][dw.com#1]. Carney warned that a vote against Canada could bring years of division and uncertainty, while acknowledging that Alberta’s grievances with Ottawa are real. He cited the proposed Pacific Link pipeline as evidence of federal support for the province. Alberta Premier Danielle Smith, who also supports remaining in Canada, argues that voters should approve the other nine questions to press Ottawa for more provincial autonomy [aa.com.tr#1][cbc.ca#1][calgaryherald.com#2]. A pro-unity rally is scheduled in Edmonton on Friday, and federal Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre is scheduled to speak in Calgary. Voters cast more than 186,000 ballots in Wednesday’s advance poll, and Elections Alberta had received and processed 454,000 special ballots, according to figures reported by the Calgary Herald [timescolonist.com#1][calgaryherald.com#1].

items.title: [Fast Company] Restaurant workers are being exposed to dangerous heat and pollution from gas stoves: study
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

When you cook at home on a gas stove, you’re releasing hazardous pollutants into your air. So what does that mean for restaurant workers, who can spend hours in front of powerful commercial gas ranges?

Those workers are being exposed to harmful air pollution levels, as well as dangerously high temperatures, that exceed safety guidelines and regulations, a new study found. 

However, the all-electric commercial kitchens the researchers studied were “strikingly cleaner and cooler,” says Drew Michanowicz, principal scientist at the nonprofit PSE Healthy Energy and one of the study authors. 

The study, published this week in the journal Environmental Research Letters, is the first, the authors say, to look at air quality and heat levels in commercial kitchens, comparing ones with gas, propane, and all-electric appliances.

‘This is what workers are breathing in’

PSE Healthy Energy, a research nonprofit focused on understanding the impacts of our energy decisions, collaborated with Stanford Doerr School of Sustainability and New York University’s Grossman School of Medicine on the effort.

It also partnered with Christopher Galarza, a chef who advocates for electric kitchens, who helped them gain access to restaurant kitchens. 

Researchers measured pollution levels and temperatures in 27 commercial kitchens across California, Pennsylvania, and New York.

That included different types of restaurants, from fine dining to pizzerias, as well as commercial kitchens inside senior living communities, universities, and elementary schools. Twenty-four of those kitchens had gas or propane appliances, while three were fully electric. 

More than two-thirds of the gas kitchens saw temperatures above the Occupational Safety and Health Administration’s (OSHA) proposed high heat trigger of 90°F; and in four of those, temperatures exceeded 122°F. 

When it comes to pollutant exposure, the Environmental Protection Agency’s outdoor standard for nitrogen dioxide is 100 parts per billion by volume. About 70% of the gas kitchens exceeded that threshold during cooking hours. One kitchen recorded a 15-minute average that was 10 times higher. 

Researchers took pollution measurements inside the kitchens’ ventilation hoods, as well as directly outside of those hoods, to assess the ventilation systems. That 70% figure came from the measurements outside of the ventilation hood. 

“This is what workers are breathing in,” Michanowicz says. Chefs also work directly above the cooking surfaces, he adds, before the air “has an opportunity to be evacuated out of the ventilation system.”

In a few of the gas kitchens, the researchers also recorded levels of carbon monoxide and benzene, a carcinogen, that exceed California’s 1-hour exposure guidelines. 

Pilot light pollution

The pollutant concentrations tended to be highest right by the gas stoves, but researchers saw elevated levels even into dining areas.

Gas appliances aren’t only harmful when in use, either. About two-thirds of the kitchens showed higher pollution levels overnight than during the daytime. The researchers realized it was from the gas pilot lights that were still on, while the kitchen ventilation systems were off. 

“It’s natural gas that is just being burned in millions of commercial kitchens overnight, serving no purpose,” Michanowicz says. 

That’s an issue for energy efficiency, particularly when the cost of energy is so high. But it’s also an issue for cleaning crews or off-hour staff who may be exposed to that toxic air, as well as people who live around or above these kitchens in cities.

Some people have been hesitant to switch away from their gas appliances. Electric advocates have been touting the benefits of induction stoves, which don’t give off excess heat or pollutants. Chefs who have made the switch say induction cooktops also work better.

A worker health hazard

These findings highlight how pollution and also heat are becoming serious occupational hazards for those who work around gas appliances. 

Nitrogen dioxide exposure can exacerbate or increase the risk of asthma, along with lung cancer, diabetes, pulmonary disease and other impacts. One researcher involved with a 2024 Harvard study had said that there was “no safe amount of exposure” when it comes to gas stove pollution.

Extreme heat also comes with health risks: exposure to high temperatures, especially over hours, can cause heat exhaustion or heat stroke, which then can cause organ damage and even death. 

“At the heart of it, this is a worker exposure study,” Michanowicz says. “We really wanted to learn more about, what does a worker experience on a daily basis during a routine shift? Putting numbers to their lived experience [shows that] maybe this is a place where we need to be thinking more about worker protections.”

That none of the all-electric kitchens experienced high pollution or heat levels show, he adds, that there are interventions that can help.

“[All-electric kitchens] are just more comfortable to be in,” he says, “and the pollution levels are so much lower.”

items.title: [ArchDaily] What Should Exterior Insulation Do Beyond Thermal Performance?
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

The buildings and construction sector accounts for around 39% of global CO₂ emissions and nearly 50 per cent of global material extraction. Operational carbon emissions which are associated with the energy consumed to run the buildings also rose by 1% to 9.9 billion tonnes of CO₂ in 2024, even as building energy use intensity (EUI) has improved. These figures point to persistent gaps in the way buildings are designed, constructed and upgraded. One important area for closing those gaps is the building envelope insulation, which remains central to controlling energy demand, improving thermal resilience and reducing carbon emissions.
